Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Recurrent aphthous stomatitis

PBM probably reduces short-term pain and may accelerate healing, but pooled results are heterogeneous and evidence for preventing recurrence is very uncertain.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact aphthous-stomatitis category contains 44 unique titles: 18 randomized human reports, 13 additional human reports, 11 reviews or syntheses, one animal-tagged record and one in-vitro record. Trials and meta-analyses generally favor short-term pain relief and faster healing, but protocols, outcomes and timing vary substantially.

Human and clinical evidence

A 2025 meta-analysis of 21 randomized trials and 810 participants found less pain immediately and on days one to three and shorter healing time with low-level laser therapy. Effects on ulcer size and functional recovery were inconsistent, and several studies used low-power CO₂ protocols classified as quasi-low-intensity therapy (Ma et al. 2025).

A placebo-controlled meta-analysis of 14 randomized trials and 517 participants found lower pain and shorter healing time, but no significant difference in ulcer-size change. Heterogeneity exceeded 89% for every outcome (Ullah et al. 2025). A separate 14-trial synthesis found that the two pooled low-power CO₂ studies shortened healing by 3.72 days (Radithia et al. 2024).

In a 64-participant randomized placebo-controlled trial, 635-, 660- and 808-nm groups had greater short-term pain reduction, and the 808-nm group had smaller ulcers at selected times. No recurrence occurred in any group during one month, so the study could not estimate a recurrence effect (AlHerafi et al. 2024).

A 2026 randomized pilot study found an early pain decrease with 810-nm treatment followed by partial rebound: 70% still reported pain on day seven, compared with 50% after placebo. The pattern cautions against assuming a durable benefit from the early response (Ibáñez-Mancera et al. 2026). An umbrella review of 41 reviews found consistent short-term pain and healing signals but limited recurrence evidence (Al-Aizari et al. 2026).

Animal evidence

One animal-tagged publication is indexed. It does not add direct evidence about symptom relief, healing or recurrence in patients.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

One in-vitro record is indexed and provides mechanistic context only.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The literature includes visible red and near-infrared diode lasers, Nd:YAG, Er,Cr:YSGG and low-power CO₂ approaches, with wavelengths from approximately 635 to 10,600 nm. Treatment ranges from one exposure to repeated sessions and uses varied fluence, contact technique, ulcer type and comparator. A single optimal regimen cannot be inferred.

Interpretation

PBM probably offers short-term pain relief and may accelerate healing, but certainty is low because pooled effects are heterogeneous and several outcomes are inconsistent. Recurrence evidence is very low. Larger preregistered sham-controlled trials should standardize ulcer definitions, treatment parameters, pain scales, healing criteria, function, recurrence intervals and adverse-event reporting.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Pain — 3.31 points lower versus placebo (95% CI 1.52–5.09; Ullah et al. 2025).

Healing time — 5.86 days shorter (95% CI 2.26–9.47 days shorter); ulcer-size change was not significant. Heterogeneity exceeded 89% (Ullah et al. 2025).

Low-power CO₂ subset — 3.72 days shorter healing time (95% CI 3.25–4.18 days shorter; Radithia et al. 2024).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for short-term pain or lesion healing

Very low for recurrence reduction

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Eighteen randomized reports and multiple syntheses favor short-term pain or healing outcomes, but wavelengths, comparators, ulcer types and time points vary. High heterogeneity and inconsistent size or function outcomes lower confidence. Recurrence evidence is limited by short follow-up and few events.
